transcript.content: Hello, welcome in — I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Thank you so much for fitting me in. Well, it’s a bit of a long story, but to get right to it... what really pushed me to finally pick up the phone and make this appointment—which, honestly, took me weeks to actually get around to doing—is this incredibly frustrating cycle I’ve been stuck in at work. 

I’m an auditor, and I’ve been doing this for a long time, so you can imagine how important the wrap-up process is. But lately, I keep starting these follow-up items after big audits, or even after these internal mentorship events we run for the junior staff—which I actually really enjoy doing! I’ll sit down at my desk with every single intention of finishing the tasks right then and there. I'll have the files open, I'll start typing, I'm totally geared up to get it off my plate. 

But then... I honestly don't even know what happens. I get derailed, or I think I finished it when I didn't, and then days later—sometimes a full week later—I'll get a ping from a partner, or I'll go to close out some tabs on my monitors, and I find out that the final email never actually got sent. Or the review note for a junior accountant is just sitting there half-typed and never got saved into the system. Or the mentorship feedback form never actually got submitted to HR. It’s just... sitting there, completely undone. It makes me look so careless, and it’s just driving me crazy because I swear to you, I always start them meaning to finish them, and then they just vanish into thin air until it becomes a problem.

Thinking back, did you have similar struggles with finishing tasks, staying organized, or following through on things when you were a child or teenager, or is this pattern something that's really only shown up in your adult life?

Oh, no, it is definitely not just an adult thing. Not at all. In fact, if you asked my mother, she would probably laugh and tell you I’ve been exactly like this since the day I started kindergarten. It’s funny you ask about childhood, because I was actually just talking to her about this the other day, and she still jokes—to this day, mind you, and I'm forty-seven years old—she still jokes that I was the only kid who could completely ace a spelling test or a math quiz, just get a perfect hundred percent, but then completely tank my grade because the big project we were supposed to turn in was just sitting there, completely forgotten, crushed under a bunch of heavy books at the very bottom of my backpack. I mean, I would do the work, or at least mean to do it, and then it would just never make it out of the bag and onto the teacher's desk. 

And my report cards, oh my goodness, it was the exact same comment from every single teacher, year after year, especially in elementary school. Like, third grade, fourth grade... they all wrote the exact same thing in that little comments section at the bottom. They would say, you know, that I was a very bright girl, very capable, but that I constantly lost my assignments, or I rushed past all the small details just to get things over with. Which is honestly so ironic now that I'm an auditor and my whole life is details, right? But back then, I'd just breeze through and miss the small stuff. 

And they always noted that I talked out of turn, constantly interrupting or just blurting things out in the middle of a lesson, and that I constantly, constantly needed reminders to actually finish my independent work. I'd start a worksheet, get halfway through, and then just... start looking out the window or talking to the kid next to me, completely forgetting what I was supposed to be doing. So, yeah, it’s really always been there, just this constant pattern of starting strong and then needing someone to tap my desk and remind me to finish what I started. It's honestly exhausting thinking about how long this has been going on, because back then they just thought I was disorganized or a chatterbox, you know? But looking back, it really was the exact same thing as those half-written emails I was just telling you about.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you been feeling persistently down, sad, or lacking interest or pleasure in things you normally enjoy?

Oh, no, not really. I mean, I definitely get frustrated with myself—like I said, it’s maddening when I realize I’ve dropped the ball again—but I wouldn't say I feel down or sad in that persistent, heavy way. Honestly, I still really look forward to things. Like my book club, for example. We meet every other Thursday, and even though I almost never finish the book—which is a whole other story, I’ll get three-quarters of the way through and then just completely lose steam, or I'll start reading and realize I've read the same page four times without absorbing a single word—but I still love going. I love the socializing, the wine, the cheese boards... I always volunteer to bring the cheese board because I get to go to this specialty shop downtown, and I just love picking out all the different varieties. 

And work, too, despite the email thing, I actually really enjoy the fast-paced parts of the job. When I'm in the thick of a new audit and everything is moving quickly, I feel great. It’s just the follow-through that kills me. But no, I don't feel depressed or anything like that. I don't wake up feeling like I can't face the day or like I've lost my spark. It's more just this constant, low-level annoyance at my own brain for not just doing the things it's supposed to do, you know? Like, why can't I just click send? But as far as my mood goes, I'm generally a pretty upbeat person. My husband actually says I'm the eternal optimist, always thinking I'll somehow manage to get everything done this time, even when all the evidence points to the contrary. So, yeah, no real sadness or loss of interest, just... a lot of exasperation.
Do you often feel physically restless or fidgety, have trouble staying seated for long periods, or find yourself talking excessively or interrupting others in daily life now, as an adult?

Oh, absolutely, the physical part is... well, it's definitely still there. It's funny you mention being fidgety, because just the other day—we have these really long, drawn-out risk assessment meetings on Tuesday mornings, and they can easily go on for two, sometimes three hours if the partners get to debating—and when I'm sitting in those meetings, I just... I cannot keep still. I try, I really do, I tell myself to just sit normally, but I'm usually tapping my foot under the table, or I've got a pen in my hand and I'm just clicking it over and over, or I'm constantly shifting around in my chair trying to find a comfortable position. Though, honestly, it's not even about being comfortable, it's just this... this need to move. 

My colleague, Sarah—she and I have worked together for years and we always end up sitting next to each other near the projector in the main conference room—she actually jokes that she can hear my leg going before she even sees me. Because I'll just be bouncing my knee up and down so fast under the wood table, and she'll lean over and whisper something about me revving up the engine again. And the crazy part is, half the time I don't even realize I'm doing it! I'll just be sitting there, clicking my pen, tap-tap-tapping my shoe against the carpet, shifting my weight from one side of the chair to the other, completely oblivious until she points it out or until someone glances over at my hands because the clicking is getting loud. It's like my brain just needs some part of my body to be in motion at all times if I'm forced to sit there and listen to someone drone on about tax code updates. So, yes, the fidgeting is definitely a major, everyday thing for me, especially when I'm trapped at a conference table.
Do you notice this same pattern of losing track of tasks, restlessness, or interrupting happening at home or in your personal relationships, not just at work?

Oh, everywhere. It’s definitely not just confined to the office, unfortunately. I mean, if you ask my husband—well, he’s actually the one who finally pushed me to make this appointment—he would tell you that it’s a huge issue at home. Like, with the household bills, for example. I used to be the one in charge of paying them, which makes sense, right? I'm an auditor! Numbers are my thing. But I would just... I'd open the mail, put the electric bill on the kitchen island, tell myself I’d log into the portal right after dinner, and then three weeks later we’re getting a shut-off notice in the mail. It got so bad, and we had so many ridiculous late fees, that he finally just completely took over all of it. All the bills, the scheduling, everything. Even social commitments I agree to, like saying we'll go to our neighbors' potluck or that I'll handle booking the hotel for our anniversary trip... he just takes them over or does them himself now, because he honestly just cannot count on me to complete them reliably. And it feels terrible, it really does, feeling like your own husband can't trust you to pay a simple water bill or remember to buy a gift when you said you would. 

And then, of course, there's work, which... well, I know I mentioned the half-written emails and the fidgeting earlier, but it’s actually getting pretty serious. The losing track of tasks, I mean. It’s not just a minor annoyance or a quirky habit anymore. Just last month, my mistakes and all that unfinished follow-up I was talking about? It actually affected a major client review. I was supposed to reconcile these secondary accounts and send off a list of queries to the client's controller, and I just... I got sidetracked by a different spreadsheet, completely dropped the ball, and totally forgot about it. When the partner went to finalize the review, the data just wasn't there. It was incredibly embarrassing, sitting in that office and having to admit I just didn't finish my part of the file. 

And the timing of all this couldn't be worse, because I’m actually up for a promotion to Senior Audit Manager this cycle, and now I am just constantly worrying, losing sleep over it, honestly, that people are looking at me and questioning whether I can actually handle the promotion. Like, if I can't even keep track of a basic client follow-up without dropping it, how am I supposed to manage a whole team of junior auditors? So, yes, it’s definitely bleeding into every part of my life right now, home and work, and it's just... it's really starting to have some major consequences that I can't just laugh off anymore.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient demonstrates a lifelong (since kindergarten) and pervasive pattern of both inattentive symptoms (losing track of tasks, failing to complete follow-through on emails/forms, forgetfulness, distractibility, losing assignments, careless mistakes) and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (motor restlessness/fidgeting, foot-tapping, pen-clicking, interrupting/blurting out in childhood). Symptoms are present across multiple settings (work, home, school history) with clear functional impairment (missed deadlines, marital strain over household responsibilities, jeopardized promotion, embarrassing client review error). Mood symptoms consistent with depression were explicitly ruled out, and there is no evidence of manic/psychotic features, making combined-type ADHD (F90.0) the best fit given the comparable severity of both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptom clusters.
